First and most important thing to know is that most games are built on DirectX libraries, which are proprietary to Windows. Wine only acts like a compatibility layer, and fails if games have any kind of copy protection reliant on Windows architecture, or check for wrappers/debuggers (like Denuvo).

Adding to that, for quite some time installing drivers was a real pain on Linux. Nvidia had at least decent Linux drivers, but trying to work with ATI was akin to dark rituals of unknown origin and results. Now it's not a problem, but it clearly shows that gfx card manufacturers don't treat Linux as a gaming platform (and they have no reasons to - only a tiny, insignificant fraction of PC gamers uses exclusively Linux for games, so why should they bother). It might change with Vulkan (DirectX 12's direct competitor) gets popular, but I wouldn't count on that happening in next 5 years.
